title: The rotation slows: inside Wahoo’s 150 ms hull study
dateLabel: 9 November endpoint · reviewed 10 November · updated 11 November 2026
revision: H0 / 150 MS UPDATE · ORIGINAL 100 MS RECORD RETAINED
evidence: Independently reviewed numerical response · provisional inertia · no physical validation
summary: An opposing moment is slowing the bow-up rotation. The hull is still rising and rotating. What the next fifty milliseconds reveal—and how the evidence is shaping our next design questions.

sections.title: 150 ms update — the rotation slows
sections.text:
The next fifty milliseconds changed the engineering question. The same H0 hull simulation has now completed 150 ms at an imposed 30 km/h. The bow is still rotating upward, but its rotation is slowing: the bow-up rate falls from 1.381 rad/s at 100 ms to 1.150 rad/s at 150 ms, a reduction of approximately 16.7%.

This is angular braking in the numerical model. It does not mean that the hull has reached a settled running attitude. Absolute pitch is still increasing, and vertical motion is still upward. Separating those observations is essential when deciding what to investigate next.

The endpoint was reached on 9 November; the accepted engineering review followed on 10 November. This dated Journal update was prepared on 11 November. The original 100 ms account remains below, with its figures and qualifications preserved.

figure.alt: Actual bow-up pitch-rate history from release to 150 ms, on a zero-based vertical scale. Rate is lower at 150 ms than at 100 ms but remains positive.
figure.caption: All 4,042 accepted dynamic samples; no smoothing. Rate remains positive. Curves break at process restarts, and accepted pulses remain in the record. The open release marker is a separate stored reference.

sections.title: A force can oppose motion without stopping it
sections.text:
A moment is the turning effect of a force. When it acts against existing rotation, it can remove angular momentum; stopping takes time and enough accumulated opposing action. At 100 ms, the completed-fluid moment was small while the bow kept rotating. The longer record now shows sustained opposition in both the moment applied to the body and the completed-fluid moment.

That opposition appears from approximately 106.995 to 138.262 ms, and again from 138.293 to 150 ms. A brief restart-adjacent pulse separates the intervals and remains visible. The pulse is not edited away to make the story smoother.

At 150 ms, the completed-fluid moment about the instantaneous centre of gravity is approximately −14.10 N·m. The body-applied moment is approximately −13.93 N·m. These loads come from different phases of the numerical coupling; they must not be treated as interchangeable measurements.

figure.alt: Completed-fluid bow-up moment about the current centre of gravity from 50 to 150 ms. The full late-window vertical range retains short pulses; the endpoint is negative.
figure.caption: 50–150 ms detail, with its full transient range retained. Negative values oppose positive bow-up rotation. Completed-fluid load and body-applied load belong to different coupling phases. A negative endpoint does not prove pitch arrest or damping.

sections.title: Still rising. Still rotating.
sections.text:
By 150 ms, the hull is 38.866 mm above its release position and has reached 10.229° absolute bow-up pitch. Its upward velocity is approximately 0.825 m/s, with upward acceleration still positive. The earlier downward-to-upward reversal has not been followed by an upper vertical turning point.

The full vertical-position history makes that sequence visible, from initial descent through the first reversal to the later rise. The graph keeps the accepted displacement scale. It describes the numerical H0 hull, rather than a board being ridden.

figure.alt: Actual heave history from release to 150 ms. An initial descent reverses near 50.269 ms before the hull rises above release height.
figure.caption: Heave is relative to release. The first sampled minimum is restart-adjacent. The endpoint is +38.866 mm and is still rising; no upper turning point or damping is established.

sections.title: Pressure maps explain where to look
sections.text:
The saved pressure field adds another layer of evidence. It maps the instantaneous numerical pressure directly onto the real H0 surface. Large local contributions can oppose one another, so a resultant moment cannot be read from the brightest region alone.

The maps use a common −15 to +6 kPa range and a zero-pressure reference. They provide spatial context, not a unique centre of pressure, an exact wetting boundary or proof that a particular hull region is defective. We keep those limits visible rather than turning a striking image into a stronger claim.

figure.caption: Actual saved physical p at 150 ms; reference 0 Pa. Common camera and −15 to +6 kPa display range. Colours are the accepted pressure mapping, without decorative relighting. No fictional flow or free surface is added.

sections.title: From a numerical finding to better design questions
sections.text:
The evidence supports a useful next step: develop controlled geometry questions before assuming that more observation will solve the design. Two priorities are the aft support region and the middle rocker, the lengthwise curvature of the hull. Their influence on early turning impulse, support and drag must be tested; changing a surface is not an improvement by itself.

Source-derived editable proxy geometry and a small planned design matrix now provide a foundation for that work. Those are geometry-development tools, not smooth, manufacturable hulls or completed CFD comparisons. H0 stays unchanged as the reference. The team must still qualify the smooth surfaces, structural implications and the relationship to intake packaging.

The intake study is part of the same system question. Its location must make sense alongside the selected pump, drive, hull interior and service access. The aft-shifted direction remains provisional. A visual fit does not establish a sealed installation or usable clearance.

This milestone therefore records progress without selecting a winner. Angular braking has developed; pitch-position reversal, stable trim and qualified damping have not been demonstrated. The model remains a dry, closed-intake hull with provisional inertia, no rider and no jet thrust, with only heave and pitch free. It does not establish physical product performance. Future geometry and propulsion studies need their own evidence and execution authorization.

sections.title: Original investigation — first 100 ms / 9 November 2026
sections.text: The following account preserves the original accepted 100 ms milestone and its graphics. Its values and next-step discussion describe that earlier endpoint; the dated 150 ms update above supplies the later evidence.

sections.title: Why let the hull move?
sections.text:
One tenth of a second is easy to miss. In a numerical hull study, it can reveal a sequence that a single picture hides: the hull moves down, changes vertical direction and rises, while its bow continues to rotate upward. Following that sequence helps us ask a more useful next question about H0, Wahoo's baseline hull.

Computational fluid dynamics, or CFD, calculates the changing flow and loads around a digital hull. Allowing that hull to move lets us follow an interaction that a fixed-pose calculation cannot show: the water loads influence motion, and the changing pose feeds back into the flow.

This accepted study follows the early response at a prescribed flow speed of 30 km/h. Only vertical movement and pitch rotation are free. It uses the dry model, provisional rotational inertia and a closed intake, with no rider or thrust. Those choices define the question being studied. They also limit what the result can say about a complete board on the water.

figure.alt: Five separated true-scale H0 poses at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 milliseconds. The 25 millisecond frame is explicitly a reconstructed accepted rigid pose; later frames use saved mesh vertices.
figure.caption: One fixed camera, origin and geometric scale per panel. Release uses reference geometry; 25 ms is reconstructed from the exact accepted rigid-body state; 50, 75 and 100 ms use saved world vertices. No movement is exaggerated.

sections.title: Water loading is a changing interaction
sections.text:
The water's force on the hull does not stay constant after release. The accepted record captures a rapid early transient and later variations, including short pulses that remain visible in the unsmoothed figures. Upward fluid force must also be considered alongside weight: a positive upward fluid force alone does not mean that the hull is accelerating upward.

At 100 ms, the completed-fluid upward force is about 345 N, compared with the model's weight of about 179 N. These are loads from a particular instant, not a settled average or a performance rating. The body's update and the completed-fluid load evaluation occur at different stages of the numerical coupling, so their values should not be equated without accounting for that timing.

figure.alt: Vertical fluid force history with a horizontal weight reference; all accepted short pulses remain visible.
figure.caption: Completed-fluid vertical force and the 178.518 N model weight. Short accepted pulses are retained. A positive fluid force alone does not establish upward acceleration.

sections.title: Down, then up
sections.text:
H0 initially moves downward. Its sampled low point is 3.777 mm below its release position, at 50.269 ms. Neighboring accepted samples support the change from downward to upward velocity. The exact timing is adjacent to a process restart, which remains an explicit qualification of the finding.

The hull then crosses its original height and reaches 6.545 mm above it at 100 ms. No upper vertical turning point has appeared by that endpoint. This is a first reversal in vertical motion; it does not establish a full oscillation, damping or stability.

figure.alt: Vertical-position chart falling below release height, reaching a minimum near 50 milliseconds and then rising above it.
figure.caption: Sampled heave minimum −3.777 mm at 50.269 ms; neighboring accepted samples support the reversal. Exact timing is restart-adjacent. Heave reaches +6.545 mm at 100 ms.

sections.title: The bow keeps rotating
sections.text: Pitch tells a different story. Absolute bow-up angle rises from 0.411° at release to 6.529° at 100 ms. The bow is still rotating upward at 1.381 radians per second, approximately 79 degrees per second.

figure.alt: Line chart of absolute bow-up pitch, increasing through the accepted first 100 milliseconds.
figure.caption: Absolute pitch rises from 0.411° to 6.529° over the first 100 ms. Accepted samples are connected without smoothing. Increasing pitch is not a stability conclusion.

sections.title: Less torque does not mean stopped rotation
sections.text: Meanwhile, the completed-fluid bow-up moment about the current centre of gravity falls from a pre-release snapshot of about 615 N·m to only 0.189 N·m. The small endpoint moment describes little additional rotational acceleration at that instant. It does not remove the rotation already acquired. The accepted analysis finds that most of the endpoint angular momentum was accumulated within the first 50 ms. That retained momentum is central to understanding the continuing pitch.

figure.alt: Moment history with a strong early transient and a much smaller endpoint while bow-up rotation persists.
figure.caption: Completed-fluid bow-up moment about the instantaneous current CG. The 615 N·m release value is a pre-release snapshot; the endpoint is +0.189 N·m. Load evaluation and body-update phases differ.

sections.title: Seeing the pressure, keeping the limits
sections.text: Actual saved surface-pressure data add spatial context. Opposing pressure contributions can nearly cancel in the resultant moment even while substantial loads remain across the hull. The maps show a saved numerical field on genuine H0 geometry. They do not identify a unique centre of pressure, exact wetting boundary or a proven cause for the pitch response.

figure.alt: Graphite-to-blue pressure values mapped directly onto the real H0 surface at 100 milliseconds, with a shared minus15 to plus6 kilopascal legend and zero pascal reference. No lighting changes the pressure colours.
figure.caption: Native saved pressure mapped to the real 100 ms H0 surface, with the common −15 to +6 kPa display range and the saved zero-pressure reference. This does not locate an exact wetting line or unique centre of pressure.

sections.title: Engineering the next move
sections.text:
The useful outcome is a sharper question: what would remove an appreciable amount of the existing bow-up angular momentum? A longer observation might help answer it, but no further run is authorized by this result or this article.

H0 remains the baseline. These first 100 milliseconds support investigation before redesign, not a claim that an optimized hull, stable trim or physical performance has been demonstrated. The next move begins with what the evidence can actually explain.
